title: Wendell and the Hymn
premise: Cyrus Underhill hosts a graveyard-shift call-in show in the fading town of Halloway, where every caller this week turns out to be someone who died days earlier. When her own sleep-recording app captures a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, she learns the dead are not haunting her—they are petitioning her, because the Underhill family took something from them in 1974: a hymn, sung at a fire that killed nine people, that bound their voices to the living. As frost creeps inward across windows in patterns like musical notation, Cyrus must uncover what her grandmother did, decide whether loyalty to family or truth to the dead matters more, and sing the hymn back before the final frost pattern completes and takes her voice too.
about_author: Sebastian Vane is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent six years answering phones for insomniacs, conspiracy theorists, and the recently bereaved. He writes horror about small towns, old debts, and the things we agree not to hear.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. On air at 2 a.m., Cyrus takes a call from Marla Tetch—who died Tuesday—and keeps her voice level while counting the studio doors, an old habit. The emotional beat is controlled dread: professionalism as armor against the impossible.

chapters.title: The Listener Log
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Reviewing the night's log, Cyrus confirms all four callers were obituary names. She tells no one, but begins recording every shift obsessively. Beat: isolation deepening; the first choice to stay silent.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Her sleep app captures a woman's voice answering questions Cyrus never asked—'She kept it in the hymnal.' Cyrus plays it back eleven times until dawn. Beat: terror curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: Halloway Remembers Wrongly
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. At the library, Cyrus finds the 1974 fire at the Bethel Road chapel killed nine singers mid-hymn; official accounts disagree on who survived. An archivist, Deen Okafor, notices her interest. Beat: the past has a shape, and it's wrong.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Hymnal
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. In her grandmother Ruth's locked cedar chest, Cyrus finds a hymnal with pages cut out and a photograph of nine choir members, faces scratched except one: Ruth. Beat: inheritance revealed as guilt.

chapters.title: Frost Notation
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Frost on her kitchen window forms staff lines and note heads—nine bars, incomplete. Each morning the pattern grows by a bar. Beat: a deadline made visible; dread becomes arithmetic.

chapters.title: Deen Asks Questions
chapters.summary: POV Deen. The archivist confronts Cyrus gently—he's catalogued the fire's records for years and knows an Underhill was there. Cyrus lies badly. Beat: the cost of secrecy; first crack in solitude.

chapters.title: Callers, Plural
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. On air, three dead callers speak over each other, repeating fragments of the missing hymn's melody. Management hears only static. Beat: the petition becomes a chorus; Cyrus can no longer pretend it's personal.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus via Ruth's 1974 diary interleaved with present. Ruth, the soloist, was paid by land developer Amos Creed to walk out mid-hymn and take the sheet music—the song held the deed of trust to Bethel Road. Nine stayed singing and burned. Beat: loyalty and betrayal braided together.

chapters.title: The Creed Estate
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Cyrus visits the Creed mansion; Amos's grandson Hal admits the family still collects rent on land 'bought with a song.' He wants the hymnal destroyed, not returned. Beat: the living have stakes too, and they're hostile.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. The haunting escalates: doors in her apartment number differently each time she counts, and the second voice sings through her own mouth in sleep recordings. Beat: loss of bodily sovereignty; invisibility is over.

chapters.title: Deen's Offer
chapters.summary: POV Deen. Deen reveals he lost an aunt in the fire and offers his research—if Cyrus goes public with the truth. She refuses; the Underhill name is all she has left of Ruth. Beat: loyalty vs. truth crystallizes into a real choice between allies.

chapters.title: Hal's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Hal offers Cyrus money and silence: burn the hymnal, keep the deed void, let the frost finish. He shows her the eighth bar already etched across his own windows. Beat: temptation framed as mercy.

chapters.title: Marla's Last Request
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Marla calls once more, lucid, asking only that the hymn be finished so the choir can stop holding the last note for fifty years. Cyrus realizes the dead aren't vengeful—they're exhausted. Beat: grief transmutes fear into obligation.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession Tape
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. A reel-to-reel in the cedar chest holds Ruth's deathbed confession: she meant to return the music and never found the courage. 'Finish it, girl. Singing alone is how it started.' Beat: inherited shame meets inherited duty.

chapters.title: Ninth Bar
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. The frost completes eight bars; the ninth waits empty, shaped exactly like Cyrus's signature. The second voice speaks directly: 'One singer left.' Beat: point of no return; the deadline is tomorrow's dawn.

chapters.title: Breaking the Silence
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Cyrus goes on air and tells Halloway everything—the fire, the theft, the deed, the names of the nine. Callers flood in, living and otherwise. Beat: truth chosen over loyalty; the town wakes to its own buried history.

chapters.title: Bethel Road
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus and Deen. With Deen and a growing crowd, Cyrus reaches the chapel ruins at midnight, hymnal in hand, Hal arriving to stop her. The frost writes itself across the ground in real time. Beat: convergence; courage amid hostility.

chapters.title: The Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. In the ruin, Cyrus reads the recovered pages aloud and sings the ninth bar herself, voice cracking, as the dead join in nine-part harmony. Hal falters, then adds his grandfather's apology. Beat: climax—atonement performed, not just spoken.

chapters.title: After the Note Ends
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. The frost shatters into ordinary snow; the second voice says thank you and goes quiet. The dead callers sign off one by one, warm and brief. Beat: release; the weight lifts without erasing what was learned.

chapters.title: Daylight Shift
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Weeks later, the station runs a Sunday memorial hour; Deen archives the true record publicly. Cyrus sleeps soundly, recorder off. Beat: restoration of trust—in others, in memory, in rest.

chapters.title: Counting Doors No More
chapters.summary: POV Cyrus. Closing the final broadcast, Cyrus leaves the studio door open behind her—a habit broken—and hums the completed hymn down an empty hall. Somewhere faint, nine voices hum back, content. Beat: resolution; inheritance transformed from debt to gift.
